processing: Green tea made in two firings and two bakings: hand fixing in a hot pan, shaping flat in a machine, then baking, cooling and a second baking to lift the aroma.
harvest_season: Spring only, mostly around Qingming, at one bud with two leaves.
appearance_dry: Flattish, fleshy strands of a glossy tender green.
appearance_wet: Soft, tender leaves of a fresh green.
taste_profile: A strong chestnut note over a quiet fragrance, with a lasting sweet return, and it holds up over several steeps.

brewing.notes: General guidance for a sturdier one-bud-two-leaf green: slightly hotter water than for bud teas brings up the chestnut note.

vintage_note: Only spring tea is made under this name, so it is sold as the current year's spring harvest, with picking around Qingming. As with other greens, drink it within the year. Older tea has no value here, so check the date.
description:
Zhen'an Xiangyuan Tea takes its name from Xiangyuan Gully in Zhen'an county, on the southern slope of the eastern Qinling in Shaanxi. This is a marginal climate for tea, and the gardens sit scattered among the forested slopes, with chestnut trees among them.

It is picked around Qingming at one bud and two leaves, so it has more body than a pure-bud tea. Fixing is done by hand in a very hot pan, the leaf is flattened by machine, and two rounds of baking finish it, the second to lift the aroma.

The point of this tea is the chestnut character, with a quiet fragrance, a sweet return and more staying power over repeat steeps than its pretty look suggests. Water a little hotter than you would use for bud teas suits it.

The gardens are registered as grown with little intervention and only the spring crop is taken, so supply is modest. Look for the geographical-indication mark and a spring date. A related name you may meet is Xiangyuan Wuya, a local green known for its dark colour and chestnut aroma.
history:
The documented story begins in 1927, when Peng Chuanqing, a tea trader from Ziyang, passed through Xiangyuan, liked the conditions, settled there and showed locals how to grow and make tea. Some promotional writing claims a history of more than 300 years, which is hard to square with this account and is unconfirmed.

In the 1970s and 1980s the county brought in Mingshan 131 and Wuniuzao, which became the main varieties. China's agriculture ministry registered the name as a geographical indication on 5 November 2015.
